# alarm selection decision record

This page has never been converted into alarm interface documentation, because what it preserves is not a finalized set of selection rules, but two trade-offs in the compatibility train that are easily conflated. The first was to keep successful and failed results separately even before the call relationships were fully documented. The second was that an old investigation leading to `khal/khalendar/event.py` does not mean that this file owns all selection decisions.

Old links still bring people here. For that reason, both the stronger claim in the initial draft and the reasons for later retracting it have been retained. Reading only the beginning makes it easy to mistake this for a record of file ownership; only by reading further does it become clear that the decision actually retained concerns how samples are recorded.

## Original scope

alarm selection was initially just the name of an issue in the compatibility train. The available code entry point was `khal/khalendar/event.py`. The records at the time contained neither a complete call graph nor material that could map inputs, objects, and results to one another item by item.

Under those circumstances, the approaches discussed were straightforward.

One approach was to associate both the old issue name and the call name with `event.py`, and write selection rules around this file going forward. This approach was easy to write up because the filename provided a clear anchor; its problem was mistaking a starting point for reading for ownership of the implementation.

Another approach was to first retain the visible results of two calls separately: one successful, one failed. It did not require explaining the failure in the same round, nor did it require attributing the difference between the two sides to timed, all-day, or any other wording. This approach was adopted.

Yet another approach was to wait until all the relationships were clear before keeping a record. It was not adopted. Waiting would not automatically preserve the failed side as it stood at the time; later readers might see only an issue that was already being worked on, without knowing why the successful result could not represent the whole situation.

The first version's decision was therefore narrow: retain alarm selection as the name of a compatibility behavior that needed to be maintained, and record the successful and failed sides separately. Here, "visible result" refers only to the selection result identifiable in the record of a particular call after that call, not to speculation about internal state.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Successful call
    [*] --> Failed call
    Successful call --> Successful result retained
    Failed call --> Failed result retained
    Successful result retained --> [*]
    Failed result retained --> [*]
```

The two branches in the diagram mark the boundaries of the records that had to be retained at the time; they do not describe state transitions inside the implementation. The successful result indicates only that the particular call left the expected visible result; the failed result indicates only that the other side did not leave the same result. Without comparable call material, these two records cannot be used to fill in shared selection conditions.

## An overly strong claim left in the initial draft

The initial draft described `event.py` as the decision point for selection. That sentence is now marked as obsolete, but has not been deleted. It explains the focus of the later review: the mistake was not starting to read from this file, but jumping directly from "can navigate to the file" to "the file owns the rules."

When this entry point was examined again, what could be reliably confirmed was that it sat within the context of an existing Python module. The top of the file showed `import datetime as dt`, `import logging`, and `import os`, and imported `Dict`, `List`, `Optional`, `Type`, and `Union` from typing. These details were useful for locating where to read, but did not provide the complete call relationships for alarm; nor did they establish whether selection occurred before, during, or after the event object was formed.

Therefore, the old sentence "all selection belongs in `event.py`" is no longer used as a decision. It was once a convenient generalization, but can now only be treated as a working assumption from that time. It is retained to prevent the next person returning through the same old entry point from turning the file location into an equally strong conclusion again.

Two things also need to be distinguished here. The file path is this page's entry point for tracing back to the code; the responsibility boundary for alarm selection remains unconfirmed by the available material. The path has not become evidence of the latter.

## Review after the card appeared

After KHL-211 became a local navigation point, the card went through failure_classified and then entered work_started. This sequence made the original records easier to use: the failure symptoms had been listed separately, so readers could first find the results retained on the failed side, then check whether a comparable successful side existed.

However, these two historical actions did not establish causation. failure_classified does not provide the internal cause of the failure, nor does it attribute the failed call to any particular alarm condition. work_started indicates that someone started working on it, not that the selection conditions, caller, or fix location have been documented on this page. Expanding a status history into an implementation judgment goes beyond the material, just as expanding a file entry point into ownership did earlier.

The review confirmed that the following arrangements would be retained:

- Retain the visible result of the successful call separately.
- Retain the visible result of the failed call separately.
- The results from the two sides cannot substitute for one another, nor should they be forcibly connected through search terms with similar wording.
- `khal/khalendar/event.py` remains an entry point for opening the code, but is no longer called the sole implementation point.
- KHL-211 is used to return to the failed-side record, not to define selection semantics.

These arrangements did not defer the issue into a generic item to investigate later. They determined how the old material should be read: first identify what each side actually retained, then assess whether there are enough facts to discuss the differences; do not first guess a cause from the card status or filename and then write that guess back into the record.

## Terms that did not become a rule table

During the second cleanup, `alarms`, `timed`, `all-day`, `all`, `day`, `type`, and `rather` were considered together. The motivation was to provide a shorter search entry point when reviewing regressions. They were not subsequently organized into a selection rule table.

The reason was not that these terms had no value. They could help locate the old entry points again and remind readers which object names or text fragments they might encounter. The problem was that the available material did not establish that they came from the same interface layer, nor that they were conditions at the same level. Arranging them in a table and then adding OR, AND, or priorities would only disguise search traces as design.

The tentative guess that "the failure must be related to all-day" is also no longer applicable. At the time, it was merely a convenient association prompted by similar wording; the successful and failed sides did not provide a comparison that could support that attribution. This guess was not carried forward as a subsequent requirement.

## Why this page is still referenced

This page preserves three historical judgments. First, the compatibility train cannot retain only successful calls; the failed side must be retained as a separate entity, even if it cannot be explained at the time. Second, the entry point for tracing back to the code and ownership of the behavior must be documented separately. Third, historical actions on the card can explain why attention remains on the failed side, but cannot replace call details.

The adjacent DOC-21 discusses long-jump walker reset. Both topics appeared in the same compatibility train, but the walker review conclusions cannot be used to explain alarm selection. This page retains that link only for navigation to an adjacent topic.

If this old decision is to be used again, first go to KHL-211 to find what was retained for the successful and failed sides respectively, then open `khal/khalendar/event.py` to check the surrounding code being examined. When encountering timed or all-day again, first confirm which side it appears on and which object it refers to; it may also be nothing more than wording left over from an old search.

The unresolved gaps remain: the existing records do not document the complete call relationships for alarm selection, nor do they confirm which inputs the failed side covers. The old draft tried to fill this gap with a file location, but that was later retracted. If comparable call records become available in the future, they should be attached alongside the specific samples, not retroactively inserted as after-the-fact explanations of the early search terms.

# Long-jump walker reset proposal

A walker reset after a long jump cannot be assessed solely on whether the operation has completed. Existing reports from the field require reproducing from the pre-call state and checking for additional visible changes left behind after completion. This puts the review focus on the state difference before and after a jump, rather than assigning the issue to a particular display result or call site upfront.

The proposal is to start with a narrowly scoped trial: capture the visible state before the call, execute the path that can trigger long-jump, and compare each item once that path finishes. The record only needs to answer two questions: did the walker reset unexpectedly, and were any additional visible changes left behind at completion? If results vary from the same initial state, retain that difference as a counterexample; do not attribute it to calendar data, formatting, or locale settings in this round.

Comparison cases should avoid treating "jumping a long distance" and "repositioning" as a single condition. Short-distance movement can serve as a starting point for counterexamples: if it leaves the same kind of changes behind, the trial scope should no longer be called a long-jump issue; if changes appear only after long jumps, further investigation can break down the timing of the walker reset. The goal here is not to prove that all navigation operations are equivalent, but to find the smallest operation boundary that repeatedly leaves additional changes behind.

The tentative investigation entry point is `khal/ui/calendarwidget.py`. The file header shows `import calendar`, `import datetime as dt`, `from collections import defaultdict`, and the locale-related `LC_ALL`, `LC_TIME`, `getlocale`, and `setlocale`. These adjacent items are enough to set the reading order: first inspect the direct handling of jumps and the walker, then revisit the use of date and calendar objects. Do not assign the reset implementation to a locale branch just because the file also handles locale.

The trade-off is to keep the trial scope small to begin with. Treating every visible change as a regression at this stage would mix normal jump results with residual changes; looking only at the final date would miss changes still left on the interface after the reset. Recording the pre-call state is therefore a necessary cost, but a set of scenarios is not required for every calendar configuration.

The withdrawal conditions are straightforward: if the behavior cannot be reproduced consistently from the same initial state, or if the additional changes also appear on paths that do not go through long-jump, withdraw the working assessment that "long-jump walker reset is a distinct boundary" and record it as a shared phenomenon instead. In that case, the results of this trial should not be turned directly into a compatibility commitment.

Open decisions: which specific UI states make up the additional visible changes, and whether the reset should happen before or after the jump, still need to be determined after reading the direct handling in this file.

# minimum display troubleshooting tree

When you see a minimum display anomaly, do not start by inferring implementation ownership from the filename `khal/controllers.py`. That is how the records here originally began: searches for both the issue name and the call name led to `controllers.py`, so the old notes treated it as the implementation location. Later review only confirmed that it was suitable as a starting point for tracing back; the actual relationships still need to be checked against the declarations and adjacent content in the corresponding revision. This old assessment is retained here because it can still affect the first step of the next investigation.

## First divide the observed situation into two categories

```text
Abnormal minimum display result
├─ The calendar count or order changed first
│  ├─ Can the input list and environment be preserved? → Fix both first, then rerun the existing test entry point
│  ├─ Only one unit changed? → Also inspect adjacent unchanged units; do not change the display decision logic first
│  └─ The input itself was not recorded? → Stop here; the display difference cannot be attributed to a code path
└─ The calendar count has not changed, but display is still different
   ├─ Is the failing node consistent? → Record the node, version, and CI job, then trace back locally
   ├─ Did it occur in only one run? → Preserve the original output and rerun; do not turn a single result into a conclusion
   └─ The test entry point cannot be confirmed? → Stop guessing call relationships and leave the gap documented
```

Here, "the count has not changed" is a troubleshooting branch, not a definition of the existing minimum display implementation. It only helps separate two situations that are easy to conflate: one where the input calendar set is already different, and another where the display result differs for the same input. Preserve the original output in both cases; if you copy only the last line, you will not be able to tell later whether the difference arose at the input stage or the display stage.

## What to retain when rerunning

Run `minimum display` through the existing test entry point. At a minimum, a rerun must leave the following four things available for review:

- The version or revision used;
- The runtime environment;
- The CI job and failing node;
- The affected units and adjacent unchanged units.

An "affected unit" cannot be recorded as just a filename. Preserve the unit names that actually appear in the test output; if the output does not provide names, record it as-is without adding guesses. The significance of adjacent unchanged units is also limited: they can only help establish the scope of this run, not prove that all calendar or all display cases have been covered.

If the rerun result differs from the first result, return to the situation-classification branch rather than choosing whichever result looks closer to expectations as the baseline. If the results are the same, that only shows reproducibility for this input under these run conditions; there is still no reason to extend the issue to other environments.

## Trace back from the file entry point

`khal/controllers.py` is an existing py module. The index assigns it the local role of supporting code reading and checks of historical behavior. The direct dependencies visible at the top of the file are:

```python
import datetime as dt
import logging
import os
import re
```

This declaration can be used to confirm the starting point for reading. By itself, it cannot establish which dependency determines minimum display, nor can the import names be used to infer the complete chain from calendar to display. When tracing back, examine the following in order:

1. First locate local declarations related to `calendar`, `display`, `count`, or `calendars`;
2. Then inspect the content immediately adjacent to that declaration to confirm whether the names, inputs, and return sites are within the same local scope;
3. Retain the small section that can be matched to the test output;
4. If moving between files relies solely on the issue name or call name, mark it as a candidate entry point rather than documenting it as a confirmed call edge.

The old troubleshooting records point here through the issue name and call name, and that still has navigational value. It does not mean that the implementation has been established as residing here. If the current revision looks different from `v_prev` in `internal/KHAL`, first preserve the local declarations from both sides side by side, then assess whether the differences can explain the test results. Do not retain only the newer snippet, and do not rewrite the old snippet in the style of the new version.

## calendar branch

### The count or order has changed

First preserve the calendar lists seen in each of the two runs, along with the version and environment, in the same record. If only the list has changed and the display output has no separate failing node, stop the investigation on the input side; do not directly modify the display logic for minimum display at this point.

If the list change is accompanied by a display anomaly, record the two observations separately. The first is the input difference, and the second is the display difference. Continue tracing back through the local declarations of `controllers.py` only if the second observation can be seen consistently through the same test entry point, on the same version, and in the same environment. If any of these conditions is missing, retain the two observations separately rather than combining them into "calendar processing error".

### The count is the same but the result differs

Preserve the complete display output and failing node. First check whether the input lists are truly identical, rather than checking only the count; two lists with the same count may still have different orders or different names. If the lists are identical, then check whether the local declarations read environment-related values. `os` at the top of the file only shows that the file declares this dependency; it does not establish that it affects minimum display. Corresponding evidence must be found in the actual output or local code relationships.

If all you can see is different display text, do not yet attribute the difference to formatting, regular-expression processing, or date processing. `re` and `datetime as dt` are both names that can be traced back, but the names themselves are not the cause of failure. Preserve the original output before deciding whether there is enough material to continue.

### The behavior cannot be reproduced consistently

The first output remains valid and must not be deleted just because the second run did not fail. Record the version, environment, CI job, and nodes for both runs; if this information was not retained, stop the investigation at the reproduction conditions. Do not manually change the input to create a third result, and do not overwrite the original anomaly with a successful run.

## Boundaries of recovery actions

During recovery, prioritize restoring a comparable situation rather than changing display values first. # palette section Migration Process

This record can still be found by searching for "palette section" and the configuration issue name. Earlier investigators typically opened `khal/settings/settings.py` directly because the old troubleshooting terms had already designated this as the landing point. This entry has not become invalid; what has become invalid is treating the hit location as the owner of the behavior.

## The old process that remained

The initial draft used a file-first verification method. Whenever the issue description contained section, config, or settings together, it went from the call name back to the settings file, then looked near the file for content that could explain palette section. When there was no hit, it was recorded as `unknown`, without inferring an answer from neighboring configuration entries.

The advantage of this method was speed. When the only material received was an old issue name, there were not many search terms: `config`, `section`, `khal`, `settings`, `get_config`, `configuration`, and `unknown`. It also avoided mixing in unrelated formatters, palettes, or other user configurations.

The gap at the time was equally clear: the record did not require retaining the caller's actual version, the entry point used by the user, or the current result after execution. As a result, "a configuration object was seen near the settings file" could easily be written as "the settings file handled this compatibility behavior." The old version proceeded under this working assumption: compatibility differences in palette section should be verifiable directly in that file.

This sentence is retained here because old links still arrive through this route. It is no longer a sufficient judgment for closing the verification.

## The order changed during re-verification

The later review did not first rewrite the configuration-parsing logic. Instead, it first reversed the investigation order. What needed to be migrated was the recording method: from file-first to caller-first.

```text
Old record
Issue name / call name
        |
        v
khal/settings/settings.py
        |
        v
Attempt to directly determine palette section

Current review
Caller still using palette section
        |
        +---- Actual version
        +---- Entry point
        +---- Current result
        |
        v
khal/settings/settings.py
        |
        v
Compare objects near configuration reading with caller materials
```

Here, "caller" means an object that still puts palette section into its regular usage flow, not an arbitrary search result containing the word palette. The reason for finding the caller first is straightforward: compatibility verification is concerned with the result of a particular entry point under a particular actual version. A filename can only lead someone to the area near the configuration; it cannot replace these three fields.

KHL-214 are the navigation cards left behind after this reordering. Their local to-do is very specific: find a caller still using "palette section" and verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. This to-do has still not been turned into a completed item by later text.

There was one security_triaged in the card history, which later became blocked. The reason attached when it was blocked was that the attachment contained only a screenshot and the original failure had not yet been obtained. Do not interpret these actions as meaning that palette section was classified as a security issue, and do not treat the appearance in the screenshot as the original output of configuration parsing. They only show that this lead was once sent for handling and then stopped because the original failure was missing.

## The position of the settings file in the new path

The new path does not bypass `khal/settings/settings.py`. It remains a fixed checkpoint near configuration reading. The file header shows `logging`, `os`, and `xdg.BaseDirectory`, and imports `ConfigObj`, `ConfigObjError`, and `flatten_errors` from `configobj`. These direct dependencies are enough to explain why the old investigation landed here: configuration objects, configuration errors, and error expansion all appear within this neighboring area.

But do not infer a longer chain from these imports. They do not identify the actual caller of a particular palette section, the version used by that caller, or the original failure missing from the screenshot. The verification record should write "configuration adjacency seen in the file" and "result already obtained by the caller" separately. The former can help continue the search; only the latter determines whether the compatibility behavior can be reproduced.

A common phrase in old records was "settings verified." During migration, it is safer to split it into two lines:

| Record item | Content that can be written | Content it must not replace |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Caller | An object still using palette section | Any search hit |
| Actual version | The version the caller can confirm | A version guessed from a screenshot |
| Entry point | The actual entry point into that caller | The settings file path |
| Current result | The original failure or the result already obtained | The surface state in the screenshot |
| settings adjacency | The configuration objects and imports actually seen in the file | A behavior-ownership conclusion |

The last item in the table is especially easy to skip. `ConfigObj` and `ConfigObjError` can serve as leads for reading configuration and handling configuration errors; `flatten_errors` can serve as a lead for continuing to inspect the error-expansion location. They are not a compatibility conclusion about palette section. The old version collapsed these layers into one, creating the illusion that opening the file completed the verification.

## Migrating old records into entries that can be investigated further

When an old record contains only palette section, do not modify the configuration first, and do not first add an explanation for section. Migrate it in the following order:

1. Retain the original issue name and old call name. They remain indexes for returning to the historical entry point.
2. Find a caller still using that section. If none can be found, stop the record here; a hit in the settings file cannot replace the caller.
3. Fill in the actual version, entry point, and current result separately for that caller. If any of the three is missing, leave it missing rather than filling it with neighboring information.
4. Open `khal/settings/settings.py` and record only observations adjacent to configuration reading. When configuration objects or error handling need further inspection, navigate around the already visible objects `ConfigObj`, `ConfigObjError`, and `flatten_errors`.
5. Change the old sentence "settings verified" to "rechecked from the settings entry point"; write the current result under the same entry only when the caller materials are also complete.

This does not require finding a complete failure sample every time. When the original failure has not yet been obtained, writing "not obtained" is more useful than repeating the screenshot. In particular, do not copy card actions such as security triage, blocked status, or an attachment upload as runtime results.

If the caller's version and entry point have been confirmed but there is no current result, the first two items can be left in place while waiting for the original output. The settings file can still be inspected at this point, but its output can only be a configuration-adjacency note. If the caller exists and the current result is available but the observation cannot be connected to the area near settings, leave the file relationship blank; do not backfill the old assumption just to make the record look complete.

The old recovery method was to return to the "issue name / call name → settings file" path. For cases with only an old link, this is still the fastest starting point: open the file, use the saved search terms to find the area near the configuration, and leave a provisional conclusion. - Old issue name only: use the old search terms to enter the settings file and state that this is a provisional observation from the historical entry point.

If recovery still produces only a file observation from the old entry point, keep the old record's status and do not upgrade it to compatibility confirmed. Although such an entry is incomplete, at least it will not overwrite the parts that were originally missing.

# Palette Validation History and Decision

When this record was first created, palette validation had only one very narrow point of focus: both the issue name and the call name in the old investigation materials pointed to `khal/settings/utils.py`. This point was easy to misread later. The fact that palette, settings, and utils appeared together in the search results did not mean that the settings module had been confirmed as the location of the validation implementation; it only meant that the earlier reading had started there.

The initial draft did not add a function name to the file, nor did it present the path as a change recommendation. This was not because the file was unrelated to the issue, but because the material at the time was sufficient only to distinguish two things: a historical lead already existed, while whether that lead could explain what the user saw was still unknown. If a compatibility record combines these two things, later readers will narrow the regression scope in the wrong place.

## Why the Early Entry Was Retained

The frozen source location is `khal/settings/utils.py`. This is an existing Python module, and its file header shows `import datetime as dt`, `import glob`, `import logging`, and `import os`. These contents provide adjacent information useful during reading: the module touches date and time, file matching, logging, and operating-system-related objects. They do not answer where the input to palette validation comes from, nor do they show what happens when validation succeeds or fails.

In particular, `logging` cannot be used to infer that some error is raised, `glob` cannot be used to infer that palette comes from a file, and `datetime` cannot be used to infer that settings switch based on time. Such interpretations would expand ordinary imports into behavioral descriptions. For this history, the file header retains only one purpose: after opening that revision, readers can first confirm why the old record focused on the settings code, then follow the actual references to determine whether this entry is still relevant.

The path itself should not be removed either. Since the old investigation record brought the reading here through the issue name and call name, erasing it completely would make the next investigation guess its starting point from the entire repository again. Retaining the entry does not give it greater authority; it preserves the direction left by a historical judgment. Keeping the entry separate from the conclusion avoids two kinds of loss at the same time: it prevents the file location from being mistaken for the implementation ownership, and it prevents the local lead that already appeared from disappearing.

## Approaches Considered at the Time

The first option was to mark `khal/settings/utils.py` as the responsibility location for palette validation. This looked like the simplest approach: the issue name, investigation path, change location, and regression scope could seemingly all be placed in one spot. Its cost was also the clearest. The old record provided no actual reference relationship, and the settings module might merely read, combine, or pass along an object; even if the file had an adjacent relationship with palette, that did not establish that validation was performed there. Writing the path as the responsibility location prematurely would cause subsequent investigations to bypass the actual caller and would pull compatibility changes unrelated to this file into the wrong scope.

The second option was to remove the path and write only "not yet confirmed." This wording would not prematurely claim the implementation location, but it would also remove the existing historical information. Readers would know that the issue remained unresolved, but not why the settings module had previously been investigated, nor whether a new search hit was related to the old investigation. For compatibility work that requires looking back at an older version, this blank is harder to use than an entry with an explanation.

The third option was to retain the entry while limiting the conclusions it could support. The path could be used for historical behavior checks and code reading; placing the issue name, call name, and path together was not enough to prove that validation occurred there. If someone proposed expanding the compatibility scope based on this, they would first need to add the actual reference, then present the corresponding call method together with what the user saw. This option still left unknowns, but it would not mistake an index lead for an implementation judgment.

The third option was adopted. The decision here concerns how the record is used, not the final ownership within the source code. `khal/settings/utils.py` remains the historical verification entry for palette validation; it is not the default change location and does not automatically own all palette-related regressions. The four direct dependencies in the file header can assist reading, but they do not constitute proof of behavior.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Historical entry
    Historical entry --> Reference check
    Reference check --> Call method: Find the actual call
    Call method --> User result: Compare against the observed result
    Historical entry --> Not assigned for now
    Reference check --> Not assigned for now
```

The state descriptions in the diagram record the investigation's progress; they are not a source-code call graph. The historical entry answers "Where should we start looking?"; the reference check answers "How does the code reach this point?"; the call method and user result are used to determine whether this arrival explains the reported palette validation. The first three have an ordering relationship and cannot substitute for one another. With only a path, one cannot claim that the call has been found; with only one reference, one cannot assume it was the behavior actually triggered by the user.

## Addition After Review

KHL-216 narrowed the follow-up work to one specific task: find the actual call behind the most recent report of "palette validation," and add back the call method and what the user saw. This is consistent with the initial decision; it merely breaks the earlier general wording of "continue checking references" into verifiable material. The call and result should correspond to the same investigation; combining search hits, configuration fragments, or interface impressions from different times is not enough to replace this correspondence.

The card later showed `rollback_checked`, followed by `work_started`. These two historical actions can indicate changes in the status of two rounds of work: the rollback was checked, and verification was started again. They did not include specific code changes, validation output, or user-visible behavior, so they are not evidence that palette validation was verified, that the rollback resolved the issue, or that compatibility work was complete. These two actions are retained to prevent "the rollback was checked" from later being misread as "the rollback proved that the problem was not here."

This addition also tightened wording such as "related to the settings module." It can still indicate that the old reading entry was related to the settings code, but it no longer implies that the settings module is responsible for validation. This change is not mere wording polish: if relevance is rewritten as responsibility, future maintainers will tend to look for fixes and regression tests only around that path; if relevance is denied entirely, the historical starting point requiring review in KHL-216 will be lost.

When performing the actual verification, first fix the revision corresponding to the old record, then check the reference relationships within that revision. The purpose is not to expand the code walkthrough, but to avoid mixing the current search results with the file state from the old investigation. Once the actual call is confirmed, the record should add three interrelated pieces of information: where the call enters, how the call reaches the relevant object, and what the user saw at the time. Without any one of these, the lead can only become more specific; the ownership judgment cannot be closed.

This decision also limits how the compatibility scope is described. It is permissible to say that the file is a historical entry and that the call still needs to be checked; it is not permissible to infer which palettes it accepts or rejects from the path name, import list, or card actions, and it is even less permissible to fill in failure text, default values, or call order. The current material does not provide these behavioral details. Writing them as common knowledge would turn this record into an incorrect premise for future investigations.

## Parts Still Intentionally Left Blank

It has not been confirmed which symbol actually triggers palette validation, nor have the validation input format, acceptance conditions, or rejection conditions been confirmed. The user's behavior on failure has likewise not been restored; therefore, terminal output, log contents, or interface state cannot be inferred from the description of the "most recent report." The specific path involved in the rollback check was also not retained in this material; only the action itself, `rollback_checked`, can be preserved.

These blank items are not another pending decision. They are the boundary of the third approach: the historical entry can remain, while ownership and behavior await the appearance of both the reference and the result. If the actual call is found later, the new material should be appended after the entry section of this record, explaining why the old path was retained, how the reference relationship was confirmed, and whether the user result belonged to the same call. Do not start a separate note containing only the result, or the path, call, and behavior will be split apart again.

DOC-26 record the mouse policy. The two materials can be used to navigate to each other, but the discussion of mouse policy cannot supply the call or result for palette validation, nor should it change the judgment here regarding `khal/settings/utils.py`.

# mouse policy proposal

When this page was first saved, the discussion was still centered on the CLI interface. At the time, we compared approaches to mouse policy as something that could be consolidated at the entry point—not because implementation ownership had been confirmed, but because both the investigation terms and the call names led readers to `khal/cli.py`. This entry point is still useful: the file header shows four direct dependencies, `datetime`, `logging`, `os`, and `stat`, making it a good place to first check what remains on the command side. It does not show a complete policy-processing chain.

The initial draft kept two candidates. The first was to normalize the input into a single policy value early, then pass only the normalized result downstream. The benefit is one fewer form for callers to handle; the cost is that when behavior differs in an observed case, someone reading the later stages cannot tell what the original input was. The second was to hold off on consolidation, let the input continue along the existing call edges, and leave the decision to the actual processing point. The cost of this candidate is not code volume, but the need for clear visibility into the return status once the call completes.

The preference at the time was the second candidate. That preference remains here because it explains why mouse policy was not immediately turned into a unified configuration setting; it should not be treated as a rule in force. The initial draft also treated "the parameter order has not changed" as a sufficient acceptance criterion. On review, that judgment proved too narrow: unchanged order alone cannot establish what the caller preserved or which layer produced the observed result.

The review did not turn this page into an implementation description. Instead, it narrowed the comparison to one CLI case. The requirement recorded in KHL-217 was for the current release to handle this mouse policy case while preserving both the parameter order and the actual return status. The card serves only as a navigation aid; this page retains the two approaches used in the review to weigh the trade-offs, along with the rollback conditions.

One distinction is easy to miss. "Normalize early" does not mean discarding arbitrary input, nor does it mean that all defaults should be decided in `khal/cli.py`; it only means reducing the policy forms visible to the caller to a single value in that candidate approach. "Preserve the input" does not mean adding a bypass either. It means that, within the existing call relationships, the form entering CLI must still be traceable during comparison. Neither description replaces checking the actual call sites.

The trial scope after review is as follows:

- Callers must not reorder existing parameters to handle mouse policy. Parameter order is part of the comparison for this case, not an interface detail to clean up along the way.
- The comparison must also examine the actual return status. Confirming only that the command did not exit abnormally is not enough to determine whether the policy was handled as expected.
- Do not treat the imports visible in `khal/cli.py` as evidence of policy ownership. They provide only a reading starting point; further checks should still follow the specific call sites.
- Do not use "a default already exists" as a substitute for the case input. Whether default values and input values converge at the same point remains unresolved.

The first approach in the early proposal was not formally rejected; the available material simply does not support moving ahead with it directly. The purpose of the trial is to first verify whether this case needs the original form, not to commit to passing every form all the way through indefinitely.

Rollback still follows the boundaries in the initial draft, now recorded more specifically: if the trial changes the existing parameter order, roll it back immediately; if the return status cannot be tied to that CLI case, do not merge either; if the only way to continue the comparison is to force the policy decision into the entry-point file, stop and reconfirm where processing belongs. "Roll back" here means removing the interface changes under trial, not that the old path has been proven correct.

Still unresolved: whether mouse policy goes through only one CLI entry point; whether different defaults are decided at the same layer; and which failure output the review should retain to distinguish input being rewritten from return status being obscured. # Quality Signal Cache Trade-off Decision

At the time, the Quality Signal Dashboard retained a set of failure samples associated with test. The discussion was not about whether to keep examining these samples, but whether to use the cache for khal-quality-signal as the comparison baseline for the current revision or rebuild the environment to capture the original run context. Here, the original run context means the runtime state when the failure samples were generated and the records visible at the time, not judgments added later to explain the problem.

There were two options on the table.

- Keep the current revision and continue using the existing cache to organize failure samples and regression tiering;
- Rebuild the environment, then capture an original run context from a new run.

The decision was to hold off on rebuilding the environment and keep the cache for the current revision. This decision applied only to comparing that round's failure samples: the existing cache meant that failure exit points from different tests could still be examined together in the same set of materials. Even if the rebuilt environment could run again, it would shift the starting point for observation to a new point in time, which would not automatically establish that it represented the same situation as the existing samples.

Keeping the cache did not mean that the cache was the original run context, nor that attribution of unstable signals was complete. This was the main objection: the cache could only retain content that had already entered the Quality Signal Dashboard; if collection and execution happened at different times, the cache alone could not replace checking the original runtime state. This objection did not overturn the decision at the time, because rebuilding the environment would also introduce new collection and execution times and would only produce another run context.

The cost of the rejected option was added to the meeting record: rebuilding the environment would detach this round's regression tiering from the existing failure samples, after which the comparability of the old and new results would need to be reassessed. The exit action was therefore not changed to a rebuild task; the outcome remained to keep the current revision without retroactively constructing an original run context for this set of materials.

The candidate rollback action was documented only as restoring the old entry point. Whether to restore only the old entry point was undecided at the time; unsampled tests were not backfilled with zeros based on the cache state either. This gap was left in the record so that "not rebuilt" would not later be read as "confirmed that there was no signal."

The attachment entry point remains at `docs/adj-khal/decisions/khal-quality-signal-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoffs.md`. This is a record of the trade-off made at the time and should not be treated as the standing rule for all subsequent cache handling; it records why the choice was to keep the existing comparison baseline rather than rebuild the environment.

# Quality Signal Stall Troubleshooting Tree

Break down stall reports from the quality signal dashboard by the observed situation first, not by who saw the message first. A stalled current entry point, an incomplete exit action, and a missing record at the standard entry point may all look like "did not finish" on the surface, but they have different people or teams to take over. First preserve the materials left by this run, then decide whether to leave it in khal-quality-signal, add an entry record, or hand off a clear permissions issue.

Keep at least four things: the latest output for the current revision, the exit code, khal-quality-signal, and the final log segment. If there is no exit code, state that it was not obtained; do not fill it in with the exit code from a later run. If there is no log window, do not substitute a summary; leave the missing window blank so later people know that collection is missing, not a step that has already been assessed. The pre-return preservation requirements for KHLA-005 are handled in this order.

```text
Current entry point stalled
|
+-- Is there a raw khal-quality-signal?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- The exit code, final log segment, or current revision is still available
|   |   |   `-- Add it to the same-run record; stop at collection
|   |   |
|   |   `-- None of the three is available
|   |       `-- Mark the missing window; do not determine the root cause; assign someone to take over the current action
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Can the current entry point reach the first broken link?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Yes
|       |   |   `-- Record the first broken-link position; check the entry point and dependency boundary first
|       |   |
|       |   `-- No
|       |       `-- Preserve the original record and hand it to the person who maintains this entry point
|       |
|       `-- Does the exit entry point already have an internal result?
|           |
|           +-- Yes, but the standard entry point has no corresponding record
|           |   `-- Do not treat the internal result as evidence that the entry point has recovered; check the broken link at the standard entry point
|           |
|           `-- Both sides have records
|               `-- Compare the position where the first difference appears; stop this tree when crossing an interface
```

## Preserve the state first, then act

The initial version only said "do not clear the state," which can easily be understood as meaning that nothing can be done. What must actually be preserved is the material from the first failure, not the entire environment in a frozen state. You can continue inspecting the current entry point, and you can also have the actual consumer enter again from the current revision; however, the new entry record must be kept separate from the original record. The new record can only show what happened on the later attempt; it must not overwrite the first attempt's blank fields, exit code, or logs.

While the state is still available, fill in the following in order:

1. Copy down the position the current entry point actually reached. If the entry point was not reached, record that it stopped at the entry point itself; do not add a guessed intermediate node for it.
2. Save the original contents of khal-quality-signal or the original record that can point to it. If only aorganizemanageed excerpt remains, note that the original was not preserved.
3. Save the exit code and the final log segment. If the exit action occurred but the exit code was not retained, truthfully record it as not retained.
4. If someone runs it again, record it separately as a new test record, and preserve the environment differences between the two runs.

This is not intended to turn every failure into a complete report. It only ensures that when the tree reaches "missing collection," "broken entry link," or "permissions issue," the next person taking over receives material from the same run. Without these materials, continued comparison of signal levels will usually mistake a later state for the original situation.

## When there is no original record

When khal-quality-signal is unavailable, handle the record gap first, not attribution. Collection can be added, but added collection cannot backfill a window that has already passed. KHLA-028 requires windows with no records to remain blank, specifically to prevent later normal output from being written as what happened at the time.

There are two common deviations in this branch. The first is to see that the final log segment is still available and directly infer the failure position from the log text. The log can show what was last seen, but it cannot prove that the signals before that were not lost. The second is to rerun immediately and, after seeing green, classify the stall as transient instability. Green only means that the new run did not reproduce it; the original run still has no khal-quality-signal, so the tree should stop at collection.

If any one of the latest output, exit code, or logs is still obtainable, add it beside the same-run record and mark which item was obtained later. If none of the three is available, the person taking over the current action only needs to confirm whether the next step is to add collection or wait for the entry point to recover. Do not write the temporary commenter as the long-term owner just because no one immediately answers about the gap. A temporary takeover registration applies only to the immediate action; the long-term maintainer may still be unknown.

The stopping condition for this branch is simple: the missing window has been explicitly marked, or the original khal-quality-signal has been found. The former is still not a root-cause conclusion; only the latter allows comparison of the entry point and exit action.

## The raw signal is present, but the entry point cannot proceed

When the raw khal-quality-signal is present but the current entry point has not reached the expected position, have the actual consumer enter from the current revision and record only the first broken-link position. The requirements left by KHLA-014 make the same point: do not infer whether the entry point succeeded from a directory, summary page, or final display; start from the actual consumer's entry point.

If the first broken-link position is inside the quality signal dashboard, have the person who maintains that section continue by checking the materials adjacent to that position in the test log, trace_excerpt, or diff_excerpt. The three types of material do not all need to be available. Preserve whichever type is available and record whichever type is missing; do not fabricate an order of events just to assemble a complete set of records.

If the broken link falls at a dependency boundary, first hand over the current revision, raw signal, and broken-link position together. KHAL is one of this project's dependencies; the quality signal dashboard side can only state where it stopped and cannot interpret cross-project behavior as an established root cause. Continue preserving the incident materials on this page after handoff; do not copy them into a separate conclusion.

Historically, there have been cases where the previous person only performed triage and the issue later returned to the actual maintainer. This change does not mean the triage was wrong; it means that "the person who saw the problem" and "the person who maintains the entry point" are different roles. The tree hands off only after the broken-link position is clear and that position falls outside a particular maintenance scope; when there is no broken-link position, remain in the collection or entry-point reproduction branch.

## The exit entry point and standard entry point do not match

The archived materials include one specific difference: the internal result contains the current result, but the standard entry point corresponding to the exit entry point does not. When this difference occurs, do not declare that the entry point has recovered just because the internal result exists. The internal result can serve as a sample for continued investigation; the missing corresponding record at the standard entry point remains an independent issue.

Process it in the following order: first preserve the original record containing the internal result, then redetermine the first broken-link position from the standard entry point. If the standard entry point can be entered but the corresponding record cannot be seen, record the position as "entry succeeded, record did not appear"; if the standard entry point cannot be entered at all, record the position where it stopped. The two situations cannot be combined as "entry-point problem," because the next person taking over needs to know whether it broke before entry or failed to leave a record after entry.

If both sides have records, compare only the position of the first inconsistency. Keep one condition unchanged during the comparison: under the same current revision, inspect the entry path first and the exit action second; record environment differences separately. Do not replace the entry point, rebuild the signal, and rerun the test at the same time, then choose a sample that looks close from the final result. That would produce only a new incident state.

When the exit action itself requires permission verification, hand the existing original materials to the person who owns the permission interface. The handoff must include at least: the position where the current entry point stopped, whether khal-quality-signal is present or missing, whether the exit code was retained, and whether the standard entry point has a corresponding record. Do not casually attach inferences beyond permission verification, to avoid turning an unverified explanation into a handoff condition.

## Handling unstable signals

When both the entry and exit records exist, but tests of the same type sometimes pass and sometimes stall, first separate the "failure sample" from the "most recent normal sample." The practice added after the initial version is to preserve the first failure sample and the environment differences, rather than repeatedly retrying as soon as fluctuation appears. Repeated retries can cause the latest green sample to obscure the earliest failure sample, making it impossible to determine afterward whether the difference came from the test, entry point, or exit action.

Change only one condition at a time during comparison. You can first keep the current revision unchanged and compare the entry paths; or, with the entry point held constant, compare the environment differences. If the comparison requires changing two conditions at once, stop first and write down the conditions to be compared. Without evidence that a condition is related, do not promote it to the cause of the unstable signal.

The quality signal dashboard is responsible for recording failure samples, regression stratification, and attribution of unstable signals. "Attribution record" here does not mean forcibly assigning a name to every fluctuation; it means keeping the sample, differences, and first stopping point correlated. When one layer has no material, leave that layer blank; do not fill it with a successful result from an adjacent layer.

If the same failure sample is reproduced again by QA, the reproduction result can be attached after the original sample, but the order of "first failure" and "later reproduction" must still be preserved. With the sample attached and QA reproduced, this only means that investigation can continue; it does not automatically determine which party should receive the handoff. Handoff is still determined by the broken-link position, permission boundary, or current action.

## Who takes over which section

The takeover only needs to land on the current action; one investigation does not need to determine the quality signal dashboard's long-term owner. Use the following format for handoff records to avoid writing temporary assistance as permanent ownership:

| Current situation | Where to continue | Materials to take during handoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No khal-quality-signal | Current collection action | Missing window, obtainable latest output, exit code, and final log segment |
| The first broken link at the current entry point has been found and is inside the project | The actual maintenance section for that entry point | Raw signal, broken-link position, and same-run test record |
| Internal result exists, but the standard entry point has no corresponding record | Standard entry point side | Internal result position and the first broken-link position at the standard entry point |
| Exit-action permissions need to be verified | Permission owner | Raw signal, exit code, and permission position requiring confirmation |
| The position falls at the KHAL dependency boundary | Dependency maintainer | Current revision, broken-link position, and preserved sample |

The "actual maintenance section" in the table is not determined by who responds first. The archives include windows when the person on duty was offline and no one could temporarily verify an action that was due; in such cases, someone can be assigned to take over the current action, but the issue must not therefore be handed to a temporary commenter. Once the person on duty is available to verify it, return to the actual maintenance scope for confirmation.

DOC-34 is only suitable for reference when the temporary takeover boundary is unclear; it does not replace this troubleshooting tree. It can help confirm who has taken up the immediate action; this page preserves the stopping point from the entry point, signal, and exit action through to the permissions issue.

## Two stopping points

The first stopping point is new evidence. When the raw signal is missing, the first broken-link position at the current entry point cannot be determined, or the standard entry point does not have enough records, stop here to add materials. Do not cross an empty window and continue discussing the root cause.

The second stopping point is an interface. When the issue needs to cross outside the quality signal dashboard's entry point, exit action, or dependency boundary, hand over only the known sample and position. If the person taking over needs permission or an explanation from another section, they should continue from that section's maintenance entry point; this tree does not replace that section's judgment.

Finally, check once more whether the record has mixed a later run into the first failure. If it has, separate the materials for the two runs; there is no need to rewrite the incident that already occurred. KHLA-023 can be used to register the person taking over the current action; KHLA-028 can be used to preserve blanks in intermediate records.

# Release Automation User FAQ

The build queue is created by `.github/workflows`. Questions from users focus on the entry point, the revision at the time, and the handoff point; artifact versions and the withdrawal window are also in scope, but haven't been written up separately yet.

**Where's the entry point?**

Start with `docs/adj-misc/faq/misc-release-automation-three-user-questions.md`. The body and attachments are still maintained by the project.

**What should I record for the revision?**

Record the revision you see at the time along with the entry point. Objects with the same name can't be treated as the same material based on the name alone.

**Who takes over?**

First, this project's maintainer should check whether the queue, artifact version, or withdrawal window is still within this project's scope; if it's outside that scope, hand over both the entry point used and the revision from that time. There are no conclusions yet on the other questions.

# Release Automation User FAQ

These three questions come from boundaries users repeatedly encounter when reviewing release materials: the build queue is formed by `.github/workflows`, work in the queue is not the same as a particular artifact version, and it does not automatically establish a withdrawal window. The project has its own schedule and maintainers. Related records should stay here, not be folded into the main project's release assessment.

**Where is the current entry point?**

The entry point is still `docs/adj-misc/faq/misc-release-automation-three-user-questions.md`. The body content users can refer back to is kept here; misc · Release Automation also maintains the attachments. When looking it up, confirm the path first, then check the object recorded on the page. Entries with similar names are not alternative entry points.

**How should the current revision be confirmed?**

Don't infer the version from the name `misc-release-automation`. After the entry point changes, retain the current revision, input, and result from the first observation; later records of consecutive successful runs must not overwrite that record. KHLB-002 contain the first record, while KHLB-003 are used to add version identifiers for objects with the same name. When comparing the materials on both sides, keep the input fixed according to KHLB-009 and compare only the revisions on the two sides; list older objects with the same name separately.

**What does the withdrawal window refer to?**

A withdrawal window applies to an artifact version, not the overall state of the build queue. First identify which artifact the question is about, then check whether that version already has a borrowing record. The borrower, start time, and return window still need to be written back to the original card; KHLB-010 relate only to this registration and cannot be used to fill in windows for other versions.

**Who should the handoff go to, and what should it include?**

First determine whether the issue is still about the queue, an artifact version, or a withdrawal window. If it is still within these three areas, hand it to this project's maintainer with the page entry point and the first recorded revision. If it crosses into a shared interface, hand over only the reproduction entry point and confirmed version information. KHLB-001 require someone who was not involved in the change to go through the original steps, and are suitable for checking the records left before handoff.

Leave anything the page does not answer where it was; the available material is not sufficient to assess other objects' behavior on users' behalf.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Stalled Release Automation

This tree starts with an observable symptom. If the current entry point has no raw records, collect them first; if records exist, look only for the first difference that explains the divergence. Without evidence of a difference, don't jump to a root cause or the last owner.

## Preserve the original state first

The entry-point records must at least let you trace back to `UID` and retain the first visible result, the input version, and the environment differences at the time. Rerunning can help with comparison, but must not overwrite the first failing sample. A green result after cleanup only shows that the later run succeeded, not that the original failure state has been resolved.

```text
Are there raw records for the current entry point?
├─ No
│  └─ Collect them first; stop at collection
└─ Yes
   └─ Can you find UID?
      ├─ No: stop; the entry point is incomplete
      └─ Yes: check focus next
         ├─ No focus: stop at the current record
         └─ focus present: check import batch next
            ├─ No import batch: stop here
            └─ import batch present: compare with the most recent known-good sample
               ├─ Match: check the entry point or environment
               └─ Mismatch: stop at the first difference
```

The entry point for the raw file is `docs/adj-misc/runbooks/misc-release-automation-stalled-escalation-contacts.md`. The adjacent incident page `DOC-37` is only an entry point to a neighboring record; do not fold its status into this tree.

## Branch notes

If you can't find the raw records, first record what's missing: is there no output from the entry point, or is there output but no `UID`? These two cases must not be combined into "the pipeline is stuck." Without `UID`, you can't confirm whether you're looking at the same run. Don't substitute a directory name for it.

If `UID` is present but `focus` is missing, keep the current input and stop at this step. Don't backfill `focus` just because a later run succeeded. If `focus` exists, check next whether `import batch` appears. Without it, the recovery action still has no usable intermediate marker; you can record the failing sample, but don't reorder the branches.

When both results are visible, compare the most recent known-good sample with the current sample to find the first difference. Change only one condition. If the difference falls within misc-release-automation's own resources, permissions, or index scope, keep investigating within the project; if it has already crossed a clearly defined interface, hand it over to the shared owner. This tree does not determine causes beyond the interface on behalf of whoever takes over.

## Old approach

Earlier records treated rerunning as a recovery action and continued down the tree once the result was green. That judgment is retained here only as part of the old incident record; it must not be used to close the current branch. Another old assumption was to infer intermediate steps from average results, directory names, or the final display; these can help locate samples, but cannot prove that `focus` or `import batch` ever appeared.

At the time, `writable calendar` was also placed near the entry point, as if its appearance meant the work inside the project was complete. It was later found that this term could only serve as one input in the incident, not replace the preceding records. Unknowns about the entry point, environment, and permissions are still kept separate.

## Stop points and handoff

Stop at the first unexplained difference. At the stop point, include the original input, version, first result, and the one condition already compared; don't just leave "stuck." If the issue is only with the project's own resources, permissions, or index, the project maintainer continues handling it. If the user-visible interface contract needs to change, leave this page first and open a separate formal review.

After crossing the current interface, hand off only the part that has been confirmed. If you don't have permission to view the entry point, hand it over to the permissions owner; if the entry point is available but the samples within the project don't match, hand it over to misc-release-automation; if neither has been confirmed, leave the unknowns as they are and don't fill in causes on someone else's behalf.
